title: Youth Poisoning Protection Act
official_title: To ban the sale of products with a high concentration of sodium nitrite to individuals, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) with 3 cosponsors, this bill classifies any consumer product containing a high concentration of sodium nitrite (10 or more percent by weight) as a banned hazardous product under Section 8 of the Consumer Product Safety Act. The bill passed the Senate on August 3, 2026 and awaits House action. Narrow consumer-safety bans on youth-targeted poisonings typically clear both chambers when the sponsor coalition includes both parties — this bill's short length and the industrial/food-industry carveouts favor movement.
summary: This bill treats any consumer product containing a high concentration of sodium nitrite (defined as 10 or more percent by weight) as a banned hazardous product under Section 8 of the Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. §2057). A rule of construction limits the ban's reach: it does not prohibit commercial or industrial uses where high-concentration sodium nitrite is not customarily produced or distributed for consumer sale or use, and it does not apply to substances meeting the definition of a drug, device, cosmetic, or food under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act — including poultry and poultry products, meat and meat food products, and eggs and egg products under the Poultry Products Inspection Act, Federal Meat Inspection Act, and Egg Products Inspection Act. "Consumer product" carries its Section 3(a)(5) meaning. The ban takes effect 90 days after enactment.
brief: Classifies consumer products containing 10 or more percent by weight of sodium nitrite as banned hazardous products under the Consumer Product Safety Act, with commercial/industrial and food/drug carveouts, effective 90 days after enactment.

top_lines.headline: New Consumer Ban
subs: Any consumer product containing a high concentration of sodium nitrite is considered a banned hazardous product
Banning authority is Section 8 of the Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. §2057)

top_lines.headline: "High Concentration" Defined
subs: 10 or more percent by weight of sodium nitrite

top_lines.headline: Commercial and Food-Industry Carveouts
subs: Rule of construction: does not prohibit any commercial or industrial purpose in which high-concentration sodium nitrite is not customarily produced or distributed for sale to, use by, consumption by, or enjoyment of a consumer
Does not apply to substances meeting the FD&C Act definitions of drug, device, cosmetic, or food

Food carveout expressly covers poultry and poultry products, meat and meat food products, and eggs and egg products under the Poultry Products Inspection Act, Federal Meat Inspection Act, and Egg Products Inspection Act

top_lines.headline: Effective Date
subs: Takes effect 90 days after the date of enactment

items.main: Any consumer product containing a high concentration of sodium nitrite is considered a banned hazardous product under Section 8 of the Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. §2057).
items.detail: This route uses the CPSA's existing banned-hazardous-product framework rather than creating a new regulatory regime. The Consumer Product Safety Commission's enforcement authorities under the CPSA apply.

items.main: The ban is limited to consumer-facing sales and does not reach commercial or industrial uses where high-concentration sodium nitrite is not customarily produced or distributed for consumer sale, use, consumption, or enjoyment.
items.detail: This preserves industrial uses of sodium nitrite (metal treatment, laboratory reagents, corrosion inhibition, etc.) that do not touch the retail consumer channel.

items.main: The ban does not apply to substances meeting the FD&C Act definitions of drug, device, cosmetic, or food.
items.detail: Definitions cross-reference sections 201(g), (h), (i), and (f) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. §321(g), (h), (i), and (f)). The food carveout expressly includes poultry and poultry products (as defined in sections 4(e) and (f) of the Poultry Products Inspection Act (21 U.S.C. §453(e) and (f))), meat and meat food products (as defined in section 1(j) of the Federal Meat Inspection Act (21 U.S.C. §601(j))), and eggs and egg products (as defined in section 4 of the Egg Products Inspection Act (21 U.S.C. §1033)).

items.main: "Consumer product" carries its Section 3(a)(5) meaning under the Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. §2052(a)(5)).
items.detail: This anchors the ban to the existing statutory definition rather than creating a bespoke one.

items.main: "High concentration of sodium nitrite" is defined as 10 or more percent by weight of sodium nitrite.
items.detail: Products below the statutory threshold — the concentration typically found in curing salts and industrial pre-mixes — are outside the ban.

items.main: Section 2 takes effect 90 days after the date of enactment.
items.detail: Retailers, distributors, and manufacturers of consumer-facing high-concentration sodium nitrite products have 90 days to clear inventory or reformulate.

underreported.summary: The commercial/industrial carveout preserves all uses of high-concentration sodium nitrite that are not customarily produced or distributed for consumer sale — leaving unrestricted a large industrial market for metal treatment, laboratory reagents, and corrosion inhibition.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's short title emphasizes youth poisoning protection, but the practical scope of the ban is set almost entirely by this carveout. Any product marketed to industrial buyers rather than end consumers stays legal, and the CPSC's enforcement calls will hinge on whether a product is "customarily" distributed to consumers.

gaps: The bill bans consumer products containing 10 or more percent sodium nitrite by weight but does not address online marketplace enforcement, cross-border shipments, or reseller obligations.

The bill uses Section 8 of the Consumer Product Safety Act as the ban vehicle but does not amend Section 8 itself to reflect the addition, leaving the ban to interact with existing CPSC rulemaking timelines.
The 90-day effective date does not include a labeling or notice-to-retailers requirement to help retailers comply.
The bill excludes drugs, devices, cosmetics, and foods but does not address dual-use products where sodium nitrite is a preservative in one context and a stand-alone chemical in another.

added: New statutory banned-hazardous-product designation under Section 8 of the Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. §2057) for consumer products containing 10 or more percent sodium nitrite by weight
